steps.title: What does a wave carry?
steps.detail: Prerequisite: energy transfer, and the idea of a medium (particles). Quick think-pair-share: “A stadium Mexican wave moves around the ground, but does anyone actually move around the stadium?” Draw out that the wave transfers energy but not matter, and that the people are the medium.

steps.title: Transverse vs longitudinal; mechanical vs EM
steps.detail: Slinky demo (Mr Lloyd prac 1A): flick sideways for transverse, push-pull for longitudinal. Students sketch both and label particle motion vs energy direction. Then mechanical (needs a medium) vs EM (no medium, all travel at $c$ in a vacuum). Finish with a displacement–distance graph labelling amplitude and wavelength, and a displacement–time graph labelling period; define $f = \frac{1}{T}$.
steps.resource: Mr Lloyd prac 1A Modelling mechanical waves; Mr Lloyd U1 AoS1 slides; Pearson SB 2.1

steps.title: We do

steps.title: Speed and rearranging formulas
steps.detail: Prerequisites for $v = f\lambda$: speed as $v = \frac{d}{t}$, and rearranging a formula. Mini whiteboards: “Rearrange $v = \frac{d}{t}$ for $t$, then for $d$. Convert 2.5 km to m, and 300 ms to s.” Check who struggles with rearranging before you teach.

steps.title: The wave equation, and what sets wave speed
steps.detail: Derive $v = \frac{\lambda}{T} = f\lambda$ from distance over time for one wavelength. Two worked examples: find $v$, then rearrange to find $\lambda$; stress units. Then a thought experiment: a wave passes from deep to shallow water. Frequency stays the same (set by the source); speed changes (set by the medium), so wavelength must change.
steps.resource: Mr Lloyd U1 AoS1 slides; Pearson SB 2.2

steps.title: We do
steps.detail: Mr Lloyd’s problem as a guided example: a wave has $f = 250$ Hz and $\lambda = 1.2$ m. Find its speed, then its period. Then students try one in pairs: a sound wave in air ($v = 340$ m s$^{-1}$) has $f = 680$ Hz. Find $\lambda$.

steps.title: Scientific notation and big and small numbers
steps.detail: Prerequisites: scientific notation and SI prefixes (nm, MHz, GHz). Mini whiteboards: “Write 500 nm in metres. Write 2.4 GHz in hertz. Which is bigger, $10^{-7}$ or $10^{-9}$?” Also ask: “What everyday things use ‘radiation’?” to surface the misconception that all radiation is dangerous.

steps.title: The EM spectrum
steps.detail: Build the spectrum on the board from radio to gamma, with wavelength and frequency arrows in opposite directions; energy increases with frequency. All travel at $c$ in a vacuum. The Sun emits mainly UV, visible and IR. Worked example: “Light has $\lambda = 500$ nm. Find its frequency.”
steps.resource: Pearson SB 2.3; Cambridge Figure slides 1B; Mr Lloyd U1 AoS1 slides

steps.title: Jigsaw: uses of EM radiation
steps.detail: Each group takes one region and finds two uses and one hazard, then reports back in 1 minute. Use Mr Lloyd prac 1C.2 Using the electromagnetic spectrum as the task sheet. Build a class summary table as groups report.

an explanation of a selected physics device, design or innovation
a physics-referenced response to an issue
a report of a selected physics phenomenon
problem-solving involving physics concepts and/or skills

an analysis, including calculations, of physics concepts applied to real-world contexts
comparison and evaluation of two solutions to a problem, two explanations of a physics phenomenon or concept, or two methods and/or findings from practical activities
